blocks.text: I apologise for the delay in starting this morning -- those who are in court will have been aware of the problem: there was a major technology issue, a part had failed in the system, but fortunately someone was able to provide a spare part and repair it. So what could have been a lot longer delay has not materialised.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We have lost 20 minutes, but the problem has been solved and we're ready to continue.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: My Lord, may I recall, please, Anna Milan.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: MS ANNA MILAN (recalled)
Examination-in-chief by MR ASTBURY
For the record, please, could you remind us of your name.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, it's Anna Milan.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Thank you. You are a consultant clinical scientist employed by the NHS at the Department of Clinical Biochemistry at the Royal Liverpool Hospital (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: I don't want to go over old ground with you, but you've given evidence already about the relevant systems in place at the laboratory. I'm going to, if I may, just by way of reminder, deal with some bullet points of your evidence last time just to put what I'm going to ask you in context, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You told us where your laboratory was located and that you would receive blood samples from various locations for analysis.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: They would arrive at your reception where they would be triaged?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: A sample would bear the name, the date of birth and the hospital identifying reference number for each sample?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: It would also have a sheet setting out the purpose of the sampling?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, a full request form.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Thank you. And whomsoever was triaging that sample would then label, in addition, the sample with your unique reference number?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Pausing there, can I ask this: at the triage stage does somebody check that the sample is properly labelled?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, if it isn't, it's rejected and obviously that's done there, it should also be done when it's sent to us as well, so it's got several layers of checking.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: So the sample itself will be labelled with the relevant information as you have just recapped?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: But also someone will check that the sheet that accompanies it requiring the various tests to be done matches the sample that it's with?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, and if they don't match then that sample is instantly rejected.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: What would happen if it was rejected?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No further analysis at all.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: When you say no further, there would just be no analysis by your laboratory?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: None by our laboratory -- and obviously there would be a report that's sent back to the referral laboratory to say "Unable to process: patient mismatch".
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: So it's perhaps more appropriate to say that there would simply be no analysis rather than no further analysis?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: So it only proceeds if that checking is all in order.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: You told us that a sample that is for analysis for Cpeptide and insulin arrives frozen?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: That frozen samples are prioritised and taken to the freezer with that new bar code that you have issued at your laboratory attached?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: But that C-peptide and insulin examinations are not treated as urgent?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Because we are an adult hospital -- unless they specifically say on the request form "Please analyse urgently", where we could try and prioritise it.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: And in those circumstances it would be tested, I think you told us, in a batch?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: For the same test for a number of different (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. That's how we operated then anyway because obviously this was a while ago.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Of course.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: You told us on the last occasion the analysis was done on a stand-alone machine?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: In a separate room from others with a dedicated operator?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Before that analysis even begins, you told us there are a series of quality control checks that are undertaken?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: There are, I think in your words, standard operating procedures which have to be followed?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. And any member that operates that has to acknowledge that they've read those before they're allowed to operate any machinery.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: So they have to be properly trained?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Absolutely.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Careful records are maintained of the machine and its — the tests that are done?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, and it's performance on that day.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: So not just a general report, but each and every time it's used, those check are carried out?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. And if they're inconsistent with previous performance nothing will happen until we are happy that the machine is performing.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: So the test would not be undertaken if there was any anomaly discovered?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: All of that process is accredited by an organisation, I think the United Kingdom Laboratory Accreditation Service?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, UKAS to us.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: You have also input from Roche, who are the manufacturers?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: I think you described them on the last occasion as a global provider.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: They are, yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: It's only once all of those checks that you have just alluded to are complete is the sample analysed? Is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Once the machine has completed the analysis you told us the results are then placed in a holding area for validation?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: And there are then further quality control checks on the machine post-testing?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Just to sort of close the batch, so the same controls that are performed at the beginning are performed at
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: the end to makes sure that throughout that time we can be accurately sure that that machine was performing.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Thank you. Once that second quality process is complete, the sample is sent to a biochemist, a human being --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: -- for a clinical review and interpretation?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that's one of us.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: So it's not simply the machine?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No. No, there's various human interventions along the way then from there on.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: And then a paper report would ordinary be sent to the order; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. If there was no action needed then a paper report is just automatically printed anyway. If it requires telephoning or if it requires an additional comment, some information to be put on it, that's the role then of the clinical scientist to do.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Okay. So paper results as a matter of course and it's matter of judgement whether the hospital is called to --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: -- as it were, pre-warn them of what they're about to receive?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: And draw their attention to anything that's important?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: You mentioned UKAS. Can I confirm, please, that is, you told us, a governing body that oversees the accuracy of the laboratory?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It oversees the whole quality of the laboratory, so it's all the documentation, the training, the analysis, the performance of equipment, the performance of staff.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: It's everything, so it governs us.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: I think you told us last time they are based in Birmingham?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's an EQA scheme. So UKAS are based nationally.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: They're more sort of global, but from an EQA point of view there is Birmingham and there is Guildford.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: They're slightly different.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: I just want to ask you a little bit more about Guildford for a moment because I think you told us last time that you're monitored?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: And that monitoring involves Guildford sending anonymised samples?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, they send them on a regular basis to see how we all perform compared to all the other laboratories in the UK.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: And those are designed to test your accuracy because you report back what you find in those anonymised samples?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. We don't know what the values are until everybody's reported their numbers.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: And that presumably is to check, again from a third party point of view, the accuracy of the process?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Absolutely, yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: For today's purposes you've been asked to comment on a blood sample that was taken at the Countess of Chester Hospital and sent for testing at Liverpool's clinical laboratories in relation to a baby called [Baby L].
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: You have noted in your statement that [Baby L] was born on 8 April 2016. Having checked the records, you've also noted that the blood sample taken from [Baby L] was received from the Countess of Chester Hospital at Liverpool at 15.47 on 11 April 2016.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Thank you. Was that sample submitted for testing for insulin and C-peptide levels in the way that you have just described to us a few moments ago?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: As far as we can retrospectively determine, yes. It shouldn't have gone for analysis if it hadn't passed all those steps.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Thank you. Are you able to say whether the sample was labelled as having been taken from [Baby L] on 9 April 2016?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I do believe, if I remember rightly, it might have just got "twin" written on it as a first name but that would have checked out with what was on the request form.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Thank you. Upon analysis within the laboratory, were the results found in respect of C-peptide recorded as 264?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. That's in one set of units, picomoles per litre for C-peptide, yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Thank you. Then we have two insulin readings on your analysis. Could I just ask you, please, to specify the measurement. One is 158.4?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: What would that be?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So that's in the different units, so that's not in the picomoles per litre, that's in what we call SI units and then the picomoles per litre equates to the C-peptide units.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: In this case was the picomoles per unit 1,099?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Were those results recorded and stored electronically?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Have you been able to access those electronic records?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. To be able to give my statement I was able to get that and the log that was attached to it.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Thank you. Could I ask you, please, to look first at what you described as a screenshot of the electronic result and which you've kindly exhibited for us as AM/03. Mr Murphy, could I ask you to put up 26987?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: (Pause)
Can you firstly confirm for us, please, that's the screenshot that you provided?
Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: If you take us through, is that twin 1?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Showing the date of birth?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: As 8 April 2016.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And obviously the unique identifier at Chester, which is the CC number in the top left-hand corner. Then our specimen number, which is the identifier that we give it once we've checked all the demographics against the request form and the sample. The date of collection is obviously the date referred on the request form as to when the sample was collected at the originating laboratory. And then we received it on the 11th.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: And then on this screen you can't see when we authorised it, but I think that was the 14th. But you've got the three results: you've the C-peptide of 264, and then you've got the insulin in both sets of units, and the important one really is the one that's 1099, because that's in the same units as the C-peptide.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: So that can then be viewed as a --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Ratio.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: -- direct comparison and as a ration between one and the other?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Thank you. Before we move on from this, where we have got the collected date of 9/4/16, what does the NK --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Sorry, no time was stated on the time of collection.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Sometimes that could be down to our team booking it in, sometimes it's very easy just to do a return key or there might not have been a time on the sample that says what time it was collected.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Are those results, were they, as far as you're aware, reported by a colleague to the Countess of Chester Hospital --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: -- by telephone in the way that we discussed a moment ago?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, because of the nature of the results they were reported by telephone.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: What can you tell us about the nature of the results from your experience?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So based on those two -- I'm just going on the bigger number for the insulin which is in the same proportion as the Cpeptide. It's the wrong way round. So normally your C-peptide should be five to ten times higher than the insulin if it's insulin and C-peptide you have made yourself. So that's why the comment on there is -- it's difficult to interpret because we don't know whether that was taken at a time when the glucose was high or low, but the only way you can get a pattern like that is if there's insulin been given to a patient.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Okay. And are you able to say from your experience what type of insulin would create that result?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, we wouldn't be able to report what type of insulin, we don't measure what type of insulin. It's just for -- any insulin that's given doesn't make C-peptide. So that's why the ratio is the wrong way round, so you know it's exogenous.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Thank you. Did you also, by way of assistance, provide a screenshot of the electronic call log information telling Chester (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We did, yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Can I ask you to look at the next page, please. Can you confirm, please, Dr Milan, that that is the document that you provided?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Indeed, yes. Sorry about the focus of it, it's not very clear. I think that's down to the IT at our hospital, not yours.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: (Inaudible: off microphone). We can see there, can we, at least if we look to the right --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, it was run -- both the insulin and C-peptide were rung by a colleague of mine to the consultant at Chester, the consultant medic in the biochemistry laboratory, and the full comment as sort of elaborated on from the previous screen:
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: "Difficult to interpret without the concurrent glucose. But if the patient was hypoglycaemic at the time it's a very inappropriate set of results."
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Thank you. At the time of collection --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: -- as you put there?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Thank you. Following that process, what happens to the sample itself?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We store all samples for 7 days just in case they want it back or it needs to be sent on anywhere else or they want additional tests and after which we do discard because we don't have the capacity to keep them.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Thank you. Bearing in mind everything you told us last time, and what I hope we've recapped in summary this morning, is there anything you're aware of that gives you any concern as to the accuracy of those results?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Nothing at all, no.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Thank you. Could you wait there, please?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Of course, no problem.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS
Dr Milan, just to remind us, you're a consultant clinical scientist --
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I am, yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: -- working at the Department of Clinical Biochemistry at Liverpool University Foundation Hospital?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: I've just got some questions about the process --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No problem.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: -- if I may. Before I look more closely at the specific process here, can I ask you something about Guildford as you told us about Guildford? Is Guildford somewhere that provides what's called external quality assessment?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It is, yes. That's slightly different from the UKAS that we mentioned about for quality -- for laboratories in general.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: They do what's called external quality assessment, so they're the ones that send us these anonymised samples and then obviously produce a report to say how well your laboratory has done, how accurate it is to compared to the average of all.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Is that done on a kind of six-weekly basis (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Depending on the analytes, yes. Some of the things that we measure more frequently will be done every 2 weeks.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Some of the things that we measure, such as insulin and Cpeptide, that are less frequent may be done every 6 weeks or every month.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Just so we can all follow this, this is one of the ways of assessing that the laboratory is performing analysis accurately and correctly, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: And what happens with Guildford is they send you -- is it in effect three test samples each time?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: And so far as you understand it to be, they know what the readings, in effect, should be for those samples?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: They have an idea, yes, depending on whether they've had spiked it or they've got a pool that they have run in themselves.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: And then in your laboratory you run those samples through your system and submit the data back to Guildford?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, we treat them as patient samples. The whole point is that they are treated like patients.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Do you know that they are not patient samples?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No, you don't --
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Exactly. So --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: But they are to test, aren't they, to see -- because Guildford have got what the results are meant to be they can see if your system is matching theirs?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: What they can look at is to check, first of all, time after time, is your system performing in a consistent fashion?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: And they can also check how you're performing with those samples against other hospitals, can't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. Other hospitals and other people that use the same, say, Roche analysis as we do and other users as well.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: All right. That's how Guildford do what they do?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Just coming back to the process that you've been telling us about, Dr Milan, I just want to be quite clear the stages of this. A sample is taken on the unit?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: We've heard that in due course that is what's called podded or sent through to the -- is it the lab in the hospital?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: So that's what podding is?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's a pneumatic tube system. It's just the fastest way to get a sample through to the laboratory.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Like the cash in the tubes in a supermarket --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Absolutely.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: -- (overspeaking) put it in and off it goes?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Then having gone to the laboratory at the hospital, in due course, if required, it's sent on to the laboratories where you work?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. So the referral laboratory, in this case Chester, will have a set of protocols, depending on the analyte, as to how they process it and treat it.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Right. If the sample isn't handled or stored correctly at any point along there, that has the potential to undermine the process, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Depending on the analyte, it can have the potential.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: If the process is undermined, that can affect the accuracy of the analysis, can't it? If it is. It's an "if".
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not so much the accuracy but it could affect the stability of the analyte in question, yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: And so we're all up to speed to the terms, an analyte is what I or what we might call the thing to be analysed?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: So insulin is an analyte (overspeaking) and C-pep --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: -- or blood glucose or whatever?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Maintaining the (inaudible) biochemistry language, but maintaining the sample integrity is a priority isn't, it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It is.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: That includes, doesn't it, keeping the sample at a sufficiently low temperature prior to analysis to ensure there's no deterioration of the analyte?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. In this question the C-peptide is stable, it's insulin -- and the only thing that would happen would be insulin potentially could go down and that wouldn't change the interpretation in this case.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Right. Just to be clear, as part of the process, that's why it has to be frozen when it comes to your lab if it's not going to be done immediately, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, we keep it frozen because it preserves it for longer.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: When the sample is taken on the unit, should it be kept in a cool bag before it gets sent to your laboratories?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: On the ward or in the lab?
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: First of all, we'll go step by step. On the ward, would you expect it to be put in a cool bag?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's very difficult now because wards do not have ice machines, so they don't have the ability, so we say, could you get it to the lab within 30 minutes, please.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Hence it's either podded or a porter will take it down.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: And then having got to the lab, then it will be cooled prior to being sent?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It would be processed at an urgent, so it'll be spun so, in technical terms, the cells are separated from the rest of the sample. That preserves it initially anyway because once the cellular material is removed from the sample, you've got no cellular activity.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: Yes. So we can get this, if we can keep up with you.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If do you that with the blood you get what's called a serum, don't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MILAN

blocks.text: And the serum is a kind of liquid without all the stuff in it?

blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Thank you. Starting, therefore, so far as the data is concerned on the second page, page 2 of 12, do we see that at the start of the relevant shift, which in this case is Saturday, 9 April, the day shift --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Having been born the day before?

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: If we can move on to page 3, this sequence is slightly different in the sense that because it deals with two separate children, [Baby L] is -- his entries are highlighted in a sort of a dusky pink or salmon-y sort of colour?

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: The [Baby M] entries follow a very similar pattern in that all but one, which relates to Dr Ukoh, are also Mary Griffith?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: And for Lucy Letby, there are a few entries relating to -- five entries, I think, in total relating to the child TSB who was her other child in nursery 1?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Moving on to page 5 of 12, there we see -- first of all, picking out the highlighted lines, which are 98 to 102, first of all, they're the [Baby L] lines. Do we see that Lucy Letby was involved in starting the infusion for [Baby L] at midday?

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: Tile 100?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: So far as [Baby M] is concerned, we have four lines, 188 and 122 to 124, for which Mary Griffith was responsible for two and [Nurse B] for the other two?

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Which are the other two children in nursery 1. That's lines 103 down to 109, with a couple of exceptions?

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Turning our attention to [Baby M], starting at 143, all entries made by Mary Griffith, these, so at 143, 162, 169 and 178, between 13.59 and 15.00 hours?

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Thank you. We see at line 216 a note made on the neonatal fluid balance chart made by Belinda Williamson?

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Which is what she told us or to do with what she told us about making up the new 12.5% dextrose solution for [Baby L]?

blocks.text: Right, yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Then we see at 218, 221 and 222 notes and observations recorded which are made by Lucy Letby for the children GT and TSB?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Yes, these are all to do with the resuscitation.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: We see that in relation to most of those, where they are signed by nurses, most are attributable to Lucy Letby and Mary Griffith?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: They include, at 228, the fact that the care of [Baby M] was handed over to Lucy Letby consequent on his collapse?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Otherwise we see many medical entries made for [Baby M] by either Dr Jayaram or Dr Ukoh?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Otherwise, so far as [Baby L] is concerned, do we see a total of five entries at 16.24, 16.30 and 17.00?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: And those are all signed by either Mary Griffith or Belinda Williamson?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Thank you. Moving on then, on page 9 of 12, starting with [Baby M], do we see the first entry for [Baby M] on the page is at 17.25?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Signed by Lucy Letby, [Nurse B] and Dr Barrett?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: There are some prescriptions countersigned by Lucy Letby at lines 280 and 281?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: And further down the page at 288, together with blood gases and intensive care equipment charts and the like at 289, 292, 307 and 309?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: There are three entries on that page concerning [Baby L] at 293 to 295?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Otherwise, so far as Lucy Letby is concerned, we can see towards the top of the page at line 267 an entry made at 17.00 hours in respect of the child TSB?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: And further down the page, 284 to 286, concerning the child GT, which are some prescriptions signed by Mary Griffith, countersigned by Lucy Letby?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Over on page 10, here there is a fairly even split between [Baby M] and [Baby L].
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dealing with [Baby M] first and the yellow-shaded boxes, do we see that most of these entries have gone to the more normal type of entries, in other words medication being given or charts being noted with vital signs or observations?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: The exception so far as -- the exceptions for [Baby M] so far as this page is concerned, in other words the ones that don't concern Lucy Letby, are an e-prescription at 324 made by Dr Jayaram?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: And the insertion of the line at line 331 by Dr Ukoh?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, and then a radiology X-ray at line 343.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Yes. So far as [Baby L] is concerned, do we see that Mary Griffith and/or Belinda Simcock, so far as the nursing staff are concerned, appear to be signing the material relating to him?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: So far as the medical staff are concerned, we see an entry made by Dr Jayaram at line 345?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Otherwise in the top quarter or fifth of the page, do we see a few entries relating to the child AW for which Ashleigh Hudson and Lucy Letby have signed and co-signed respectively?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Thank you. Then the final page, please. This covers the period of time from 20.02 hours to 21.26. For [Baby M] do we see that Mary Griffith, her name appears but that's because it relates to nursing notes that she was making at this time concerning what had happened to [Baby M] --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: -- earlier in the shift? Otherwise, so far as [Baby M] was concerned, and with the exception of the single entry made by Dr Ukoh, do we see that this page really concerns nursing note updates made by Lucy Letby?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: So far as [Baby L] is concerned, do we have a similar picture but that this time it's only Mary Griffith, but these all relate to nursing note updates?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, correct.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Thank you. We then have the other two children in nursery 1, GT and TSB, and do we see a similar position given that this is after the shift has nominally ended after 8 pm, that these are all nursing note updates made by Lucy Letby in respect of those two children?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: TYNDALL

blocks.text: Thank you very much. I don't know whether there are -- no, there are no further questions for you.

blocks.text: No, thank you very much.
